newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Analysts shocked by new P&U warning.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts shocked by new P&U warning.

text.p: A new profit warning from Swedish/U.S. drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn (P&U) hit analysts from out of the blue on Wednesday and the company's share price plummeted.
P&U released a statement saying its sales fell by six percent in the first quarter of 1997 and earnings per share before non-recurring items were expected to drop by around 16 percent.
The group's shares plunged on the news, diving 39 crowns to 234 crowns by 1310 GMT.
"It was a profit warning and it was unexpected," UBS analyst Birgit Kullhoff said in an initial reaction to the news.
"A profit warning is always bad news."
Some analysts were waiting for hear what the company had to say at an analysts' telephone conference call, due to take place around 1300 GMT, before commenting on the statement.
Kulhoff said she would wait until after the conference call before deciding on any changes to her recommendations on the stock.
The markets have been unpleasantly surprised several times in the past by P&U, formed in November 1995 by a merger between Michigan based Upjohn and Sweden's Pharmacia.
An analyst from a London-based securities house said P&U's problem was that its product portfolio was too mature and it needed to throw its weight behind new products.
"The problem is that there are not too many new products," he said.
"Given that this is the fourth profit warning it is not a one-off," the analyst. "I just hope it is the last."
P&U attributed the first quarter sales shortfall to adverse exchange rate movements and customer inventory adjustments after a strong final quarter in 1996.
Weaker demand in Europe, particularly Germany and Sweden, and generic competition in the U.S. also ate into sales, the company said.
Chief financial officer Bob Salisbury told journalists on a telephone conference call that some of the negative factors seen hitting the first quarter were not expected to continue.
"Some of the factors will moderate and not have as adverse an effect on results in following quarters," Salisbury said.
However he refused to give forecasts for the rest of the year.
"We don't give detailed forecasts," he said. "There is still a fair amount of uncertainty."
